name: Magnesium threonate

lead: Magnesium threonate is a supplement form of magnesium marketed as raising magnesium levels in the brain. People add it to bedtime routines for calm, sleep and focus, with the payoff of better recovery and a more rested look.

The idea comes from a 2010 rat study linking raised brain magnesium to more synapses and better learning, described in a Neuron commentary. Human trials in older adults, people with ADHD, healthy adults and athletes have been registered, but the entries reviewed do not report results.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or powder in the evening, often with apigenin and theanine in a sleep stack. Users judge it by sleep over a few weeks.
Excess oral magnesium most often causes diarrhea, and high blood levels mostly occur with kidney dysfunction. Threonate-specific safety data are limited, and it is sold as a dietary supplement.

web.title: Magtein formula in healthy Chinese adults 2022

angle.text: People take this brain-targeted magnesium salt in the evening for sleep and calm, as part of recovery routines that support skin and energy. The idea comes from a rat study; human sleep trials are registered but results are not published in the sources reviewed.

lead: Magnesium L-threonate is a salt of magnesium and threonic acid, a metabolite of vitamin C, sold as an oral dietary supplement under names such as Magtein. It is marketed as a form of magnesium intended to raise magnesium levels in the brain, and in appearance and recovery communities it is taken mainly in the evening for sleep, calm and cognition rather than for any direct effect on facial or bodily features.

The idea behind the product comes from a 2010 study in Neuron, in which rats given magnesium L-threonate showed higher brain magnesium, denser hippocampal synapses and improved learning and memory [1][2]. Human research has since grown: randomised placebo-controlled trials have reported on sleep quality and daytime functioning in adults with self-reported sleep problems, on cognition in healthy adults, and on pain in cancer patients, alongside several newer registered studies in athletes and other groups [3][4][5][6][7].

Magnesium in general is an established nutrient, and excess oral magnesium most commonly causes diarrhea [8]. Whether the threonate form delivers more magnesium to the brain than other forms in people has not been measured in the human trials, and a 2026 rat study reported higher magnesium in tissues with magnesium acetyl taurate than with threonate [9].

It appears in bedtime and recovery routines among lifters and appearance-focused readers, who describe it as part of a stack aimed at better sleep and calm, the idea being that more restful nights support training, skin and general presentation.[10][11]

paras: Magnesium L-threonate is sold for memory, mood, stress and sleep. In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is usually added to bedtime supplement routines, on the premise that better sleep supports skin, energy and general appearance.

Magnesium ions block the NMDA-type glutamate receptor channel and reduce nerve cell activity at high concentrations [8]. A 2010 commentary on rat experiments described oral magnesium threonate as raising brain magnesium and increasing hippocampal NR2B expression and synapse density, accompanied by better cognition in young and old rats over 12 to 24 days [2]. Later rodent work has also studied the compound, for example a 2023 preprint reporting changes in the urine proteome of rats after short-term intake [12]. A 2016 review of magnesium in the nervous system noted a long-standing interest in neuroprotective roles but that translation to clinical use has been difficult [13].

The 2010 Neuron paper reported that rats given the compound had more functional presynaptic release sites with lower release probability, and increased NR2B-containing NMDA receptors and downstream signalling, which the authors link to enhanced synaptic plasticity [1]. These are results in animals; whether the same synaptic changes occur in people has not been measured.

Magnesium L-threonate is the magnesium salt of L-threonic acid, with the formula Mg(C4H7O5)2 and a molar mass of about 294.5 g/mol; it is classed with other magnesium supplements under the ATC code A12.[14] Wikipedia describes it as reported to cross the blood-brain barrier more readily than ordinary magnesium ions, a claim attached to the branded form Magtein.[14]

Threonic acid is a metabolite of vitamin C, and the compound is sold as capsules and powders, alone or combined with other magnesium forms and sleep ingredients, as in the registered stress-and-sleep supplement combination study.[15][14]

The popular rationale traces to a 2010 paper in Neuron by Inna Slutsky and colleagues, which introduced magnesium-L-threonate, reporting that oral intake raised brain magnesium in rats, increased synaptic density markers in the hippocampus and improved learning and memory, including pattern completion in aged rats; a Neuron commentary titled Kalzium ist nicht alles (Calcium is not everything) discussed it [1][2]. A 2025 mouse study reported improved memory and more new neurons in an Alzheimer's model with the compound [16].

Human testing began with small, mostly registered trials: a 2012 study of the branded form in 50 older adults, dementia and ADHD pilots in 2014 and 2016 [17][18][19]. Published randomised trials followed, including a 2022 study of a Magtein-based formula in 109 healthy Chinese adults, a 2024 sleep trial in 80 adults and a 2025 trial in 100 adults, with newer sleep, recovery and athlete studies registered from 2025 [20][21][22][3][4][5].

Its spread to fitness and wellness audiences accelerated after podcast host Andrew Huberman discussed magnesium threonate as part of a sleep supplement set alongside L-theanine and apigenin; forum users cite him directly as their reason for choosing the threonate form over glycinate.[23][24]

sections.h: Use in lifting and appearance communities
paras: On T Nation, members mention magnesium threonate in brain stacks, in bedtime routines with L-theanine, and in sleep-support lists alongside melatonin, glycine and other items, often adding that they are unsure how much it contributes.[10][24][25] One user wrote that he takes it before bed and added zinc and ZMA to his routine, while another says he combines it with creatine for fitness purposes.[26][11]

The link to looks is indirect and runs through sleep and recovery: better sleep is associated with training performance and general well-being, and proponents expect magnesium to contribute to calm and sleep onset. Whether the threonate form does so in humans is the subject of the registered trials above.

Several T Nation users cite sleep as the reason for taking the supplement, and one notes combining it with L-theanine without being sure of the contribution [24]. The 2024 and 2025 randomised trials reported sleep and daytime-functioning outcomes in adults with sleep complaints, which is the closest published match to how the community uses it [3][4].

sections.h: How it connects to looking better
paras: The appearance case for magnesium threonate runs through sleep, stress and recovery. People who use it say that better-quality sleep supports skin condition, training recovery and the energy to keep up a routine, so the supplement is added to an evening stack in the hope of those downstream benefits.[23][24] This is a chain of reasoning offered by users rather than an outcome measured in the threonate trials, which have looked at cognition, mood, sleep and dementia rather than skin or physique.[17][18][22]

Magnesium in general has a more settled role: it is an essential mineral involved in nerve and muscle function, and reference summaries list fatigue, weakness, cramps and tremor among the signs of deficiency.[27][8] Some in lifting communities take magnesium to cover low dietary intake, and the threonate salt is chosen specifically because of the rodent finding that it raised brain magnesium.[2][10]

Magnesium supplements come in many salts. Reference summaries note that oxide is magnesium-dense but less bioavailable than citrate, chloride, lactate or aspartate in the trials discussed, and that amino-acid chelates were less bioavailable in one study.[27] The branded form Magtein is the one used in at least one registered human study.[17][14] No head-to-head trial comparing threonate with glycinate or citrate for sleep has been identified.

The deficiency summary estimates that a majority of people in the United States do not meet the recommended magnesium intake, with leafy greens, beans, nuts, seeds and unrefined grains as the main food sources.[27] That dietary context is the usual starting point for those who add any form of magnesium.

The 2010 Neuron paper presented magnesium-L-threonate as a newly developed compound for raising brain magnesium [1], and a 2026 rat study comparing it with magnesium acetyl taurate reported higher tissue magnesium with the latter and a combined group [9]. No human head-to-head comparison of threonate with glycinate or citrate has been identified.

Mentions cluster in brain-function, sleep and testosterone-optimisation threads on T Nation, where users compare it with glycinate and often attribute their choice of the threonate form to podcast discussion.[10][11][23][24][26] Some posters report subjective improvements in sleep or mood, while others list it as one item among several changes made at once, which makes its individual contribution hard to separate even by their own account.[24][25]

Sleep. A 2024 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 80 adults aged 35 to 55 with self-assessed sleep problems for 21 days and reported that the magnesium threonate group maintained sleep quality and daytime functioning while the placebo group declined; scores on questionnaires such as the Insomnia Severity Index and on Oura ring measures including deep sleep and REM sleep score favoured the supplement group, as did self-reported energy and productivity [3]. A corrigendum to this paper was published in 2025 [3].

Cognition. A 2025 six-week randomised trial in 100 adults aged 18 to 45 with dissatisfied sleep reported greater improvement in the NIH Total Cognition Composite (p = 0.043), larger effects on working and episodic memory, an estimated 7.5-year reduction in brain cognitive age and faster reaction time versus placebo, with no group difference on the Raven's matrices test and a greater improvement in self-reported sleep-related impairment [4]. A 2022 trial of a Magtein formula that also contained phosphatidylserine and vitamins C and D reported improved memory quotient scores in 109 healthy adults over 30 days, with larger gains in older participants; the formula, not threonate alone, was tested [5].

Pain. In a randomised trial of 109 breast cancer surgery patients, the group given the compound for 12 weeks had a smaller rise in pain scores at six months than controls, although 31% versus 26% of the groups reported chronic pain [6]. A randomised trial in 83 advanced cancer patients on opioids reported smaller increases in daily morphine dose from day 30 and relief of opioid-induced constipation with the compound versus placebo [7].

Registered studies. Earlier registered trials include a Magtein trial in 50 older adults begun in 2012, a dementia pilot (17 participants) and an ADHD trial (20 participants) [17][18][19]. Newer registrations cover sleep, recovery and performance in 109 collegiate athletes and a planned athlete study of 150, sex differences in sleep, cognition and neuromuscular function in 81 healthy adults, sleep after knee arthroplasty, and menopausal symptoms [20][21][22][28][29].

Animal work. Rat and mouse studies have examined the compound in learning, Alzheimer's models and hypothyroid rats, where one study found reduced hippocampal amyloid load without cognitive improvement and another compared it with magnesium acetyl taurate [9][30][16]. A 2025 comprehensive review of magnesium in depression, migraine and cognitive health describes the broader literature as heterogeneous [31].

For magnesium supplements generally, diarrhea is the most common symptom of excess oral intake, poisoning is very rare with normal kidney function, and high blood magnesium usually results from kidney dysfunction [8]. The US tolerable upper intake level for supplemental magnesium is 350 mg per day and the European limit is 250 mg per day, according to Wikipedia [8]. Safety data specific to the threonate form are limited.

It is commonly listed alongside apigenin and theanine in bedtime stacks; see the entry on the Huberman sleep stack. Dietary supplements as a category are not approved by regulators for treating conditions before sale.

Trials of branded formulations such as Magtein PS (with phosphatidylserine and vitamins) appear in the literature alongside generic threonate products [5]. As with other dietary supplements, products are not pre-approved by regulators for treating conditions before sale.

lore.intro: Magnesium threonate is discussed as the brain form of magnesium and a common bedtime addition in sleep stacks, frequently attributed to Andrew Huberman's sleep recommendations.[23][24]

claims.claim: Threonate crosses into the brain better than other magnesium forms
It supports recovery and athletic performance
It treats pain or helps with opioid use.

timeline.event: Slutsky and colleagues report magnesium-L-threonate raising brain magnesium and improving learning in rats (Neuron) [1][2].
Trial of Magtein in older adults begins [17].
Pilot trial in people with dementia begins [18].
Trial of a Magtein-based formula reports memory gains in 109 healthy Chinese adults [5].
Randomised trials report outcomes in post-mastectomy pain and in opioid use in advanced cancer [6][7].
Randomised trial in 80 adults reports improved sleep quality and daytime functioning [3].
Randomised cognition and sleep trial in 100 adults published; sleep and athlete trials registered [4][20][21][22].
